title: After Christendom: A Study on Post-Christian Faith
subtitle: A five-session study on following Jesus faithfully in a world that no longer pretends to be Christian.
summary:
This study is for Christians who can feel the ground moving, for pastors who aren't sure what their church is for anymore, and for small groups willing to look at the present as it is instead of mourning a past that was never as Christian as we remember. Its five sessions ask what has actually ended and why that may be a mercy; how Jeremiah taught the captives in Babylon to live; how the church bore witness before it had any power; what it means to be a creative minority instead of a defeated one; and what hope looks like when it stops looking backward. A volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer.

It won't tell the church to fight harder to win back a culture that has moved on, and it won't hold a funeral either. Panic and denial are the two easy roads, and both are dead ends. Cultural Christianity is ending. But the end of Christendom isn't the end of the church. The church started on the far side of Christendom, small and strange and without a single law on its side, and it turned the Roman world upside down. We built more on the culture than on Christ than we'd like to admit, and this study starts there.
audience: Thoughtful Christians, pastors, and small groups in a secular age

sessions.title: The End of Christendom
sessions.aim: To name what has ended without panic and without denial, to see that what's passing is the cultural scaffolding around the faith and not the faith itself, and to ask whether losing Christendom might be a mercy.
sessions.summary:
Many Christians say they want their country back: the one where stores closed on Sunday, where a prayer opened the school day, where being a decent person and being a Christian were assumed to be the same thing. The grief is understandable. But that country also taught a great many people they were Christians who had never met Christ.

Two answers compete. One says this is a catastrophe, and it's right that real goods are passing; a society shaped by the memory of the gospel restrained cruelties that are coming back. The other says good riddance, and it's right that the marriage of faith and power did real harm and filled churches with people who were never converted.

Christendom wasn't the gospel, and it wasn't nothing. It was a long arrangement, begun in the fourth century, in which the culture did much of the church's work for it. That arrangement is ending. This session asks what we've actually lost, and what the church becomes when the culture stops carrying it.

keyScripture.why: "Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul" (1 Peter 2:11). Peter tells the church it lives in the world as resident aliens, not owners. That's the status we're recovering.

discussion.q: When you hear that Christendom is ending, what's your first reaction? Grief, relief, fear, or something you'd rather not say out loud?
discussion.behind: Get the gut reaction on the table before any analysis. Many people carry a fear they've been told is faithless, or a relief they've been told is disloyal. Don't settle anything yet. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Christianity and Christendom aren't the same thing. One is the faith; the other is the cultural arrangement that carried it. How much of what you took for faith may have been the culture carrying it for you?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. Keep it personal, not a history lecture. Most of us inherited a faith the culture propped up, and we haven't yet found out how much of it is ours. Go first, and keep it gentle.

discussion.q: Where have you seen cultural Christianity stand in for the real thing, in a town, a family, or a church?
discussion.behind: Move from nostalgia toward discernment without mocking the past. A culture that makes Christianity easy and respectable also tends to make it cheap. Help people name the difference between a Christian-shaped society and a converted heart.

discussion.q: Some real goods are passing with Christendom. What do you genuinely grieve, and how do you grieve it without mistaking it for the gospel?
discussion.behind: Don't let the room swing to "good riddance." Some of what's ending was a mercy to real people. The work is to grieve it while refusing to call the arrangement the kingdom of God.

discussion.q: Where might you, your church, or your own faith have been built more on the culture than on Christ?
discussion.behind: End by bringing it home, starting with yourself. This isn't a time to confess other people's failures. Go first.

objections.objection: The end of Christendom is a disaster. A Christian civilization is collapsing, the culture is openly hostile, and the only faithful response is to fight to win it back.
objections.response: Half of this is true. A society that remembered the gospel, even dimly, restrained some cruelties, honored some weak people, and made some virtues plausible, and what's replacing it isn't obviously better. The grief isn't foolish. But the thing being defended isn't the gospel. It's Christendom, the arrangement in which the culture did the church's work, and that arrangement produced crowds of people who thought being respectable was the same as being saved. The early church had no civilization to defend and no power to lose, and it turned the Roman world upside down. Grieve the goods. Don't spend the church's strength defending the scaffolding.

objections.objection: Good riddance. Christendom was always a corruption, the church in bed with empire, blessing wars and kings. The faster it dies, the purer the church will be.
objections.response: Much of that is right. The marriage of faith and political power produced crusades, inquisitions, and state churches that persecuted dissenters, and it baptized people into a culture who never met Christ. The church should repent of all of it. But the same arrangement also carried hospitals, universities, and the slow softening of a brutal world by the memory of a crucified God. And relief at its passing can be its own pride. Losing power doesn't make a church holy. It removes one set of temptations and exposes us to others.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the culture stopped carrying your faith along, making it easy and respectable, how much of it do you think would remain?
sessions.practice: This week, take a quiet inventory. Write down the parts of your Christian life that depend on the culture cooperating: the calendar, the social expectations, the sense that being a good neighbor and being a believer are the same thing. Beside each one, ask: if this support disappeared tomorrow, would my faith here survive on its own? Don't fix anything yet. Just look at what you find.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've grieved the passing of a Christian culture, and some of that grief is right, because real goods are leaving with it. But we confess we've often loved the arrangement more than we loved you. We leaned on the culture to do what you gave the church to do, and we called ourselves yours because the world around us made it easy. Forgive us. Teach us to grieve what was good without clutching it as if it were the gospel, and to find out what of our faith is truly ours and truly yours. Make us exiles who know whose we are. Amen.
reflection: What have I taken for faith that may only have been the culture holding it up, and what happens to it now?
What real goods am I grieving as Christendom ends, and how do I honor that grief without confusing the arrangement with the kingdom of God?
If the early church turned the world upside down with no power at all, where have I been looking for the church's strength?
sessions.teaching:
A lot of Christians say they want their country back. They mean the country where stores closed on Sunday, where the school day opened with a prayer, where being a decent person and being a Christian were assumed to be roughly the same thing and nobody asked you to explain why you believed. I understand the grief, and I've felt some of it. But something hard has to be said to it. That country taught a great many people they were Christians who had never met Christ. So I don't want to start where most of us want to start, with how to win the culture back. I want to start with a plainer question: what have we actually lost?

There are two answers, and each wants to silence the other. The first says this is a catastrophe. A Christian civilization is collapsing, the culture has turned hostile, and the faithful response is to resist and recover the ground before it's gone. That isn't simply wrong. A society that remembered the gospel, even faintly, restrained some cruelties and honored some weak people and made some virtues plausible that are now becoming hard to imagine. What's replacing that memory isn't obviously better, and in places it's worse. Grieving that isn't foolish.

The second answer says good riddance. Christendom was a corruption from the start: the church climbing into bed with empire, blessing kings and wars, filling its buildings with people who were baptized into a culture and never converted to a Lord. That isn't wrong either. The marriage of faith and political power did terrible things, and the church should repent of them without flinching. Crowds of merely cultural Christians were a spiritual problem, not a victory.

Here's the distinction that matters. Christendom was not the gospel. It was an arrangement, and it had a beginning you can date. In the fourth century the emperor Constantine made the faith first legal and then favored, and over the centuries that followed a civilization grew up in which the culture did much of the church's work for it. Belief became the path of least resistance. People were carried along on borrowed momentum. That's what is ending, not Christ but the scaffolding.

But Christendom wasn't nothing, either. The same arrangement carried real mercy into a brutal world. It built hospitals and universities, and it slowly bent a violent culture toward the memory of a God who was crucified rather than a god who conquered. To wave all of that away as corruption is to lie about the good that was there.

So the right posture toward its passing isn't panic and it isn't triumph. It's grief and relief at once: grief for what was good, relief at the chance to be the church again without the culture doing our work for us.

We're inside this. Many of us built more of our churches on cultural Christianity than on Christ. We counted the people who came because it was respectable to come, and we called it fruit. We assumed an America that would always be vaguely on our side, and we built as if that assumption were the gospel. The end of Christendom is finding the whole church out, and that's exactly where the mercy is.

Peter wrote to Christians scattered across the provinces of Asia Minor and called them "sojourners and exiles" (1 Peter 2:11). He didn't think of the church as the owner of its culture. The church he knew had no emperor, no respectability, no laws on its side, and no cultural current carrying anyone anywhere. It was a small, strange minority in a hostile empire, and it turned that empire upside down. The question for us isn't how to get the scaffolding back. It's whether we still know how to be that church.

scriptureStudy.note: "I urge you as sojourners and exiles." Peter assumes the church lives as resident aliens in a culture that isn't its own. That's the self-understanding the end of Christendom hands back to us.
Peter writes "To those who are elect exiles of the dispersion." From the first verse the church is a scattered, chosen minority, not the established religion of a society.
"But our citizenship is in heaven." Paul wrote that to a proud Roman colony. The church's first allegiance was never to the empire around it, a truth Christendom blurred.
"My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting." The kingdom doesn't advance by seizing the levers of power.

"The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened." Small, hidden, and working through the whole, which is how the early church actually spread.
"But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food." He served Babylon and still kept a line he wouldn't cross: present in the empire without belonging to it.
"For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come." The church was never promised a permanent home in any earthly order, so losing one isn't losing its true home.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up the history, because "Christendom" gets used as if it were eternal. For roughly its first three centuries the church had no political power. It was a suspect and often persecuted minority. The historian Alan Kreider, in The Patient Ferment of the Early Church (2016), argues that it grew without programs or pressure, through the patient, attractive strangeness of communities that loved their enemies, cared for the abandoned, and formed new believers slowly, sometimes over years, before baptism.

Then came the fourth century and what historians call the Constantinian shift. Where it had once cost something to be a Christian, in time it cost something not to be one. The church gained power, property, and respectability, and lost some of the conditions that had made it compelling. Hold both sides: Christendom did real good for centuries, and it also replaced conversion with conformity in many places. Set Kreider's early church beside the Christendom church and ask which one we're more like, and which one the gospel requires.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a pastor in a town where nearly everyone used to go to church somewhere watches that habit fade over a generation. He's faithful and thoughtful, and he responds the way many do. He worries about the numbers, doubles down on the programs that filled the building twenty years ago, and preaches more and more about the culture's decline. The harder he pushes, the older, smaller, and angrier the congregation becomes. Then his grown daughter tells him over a hard dinner that she still loves Jesus but can't stand what the church has become: a fortress of grievance with the doors shut.

It undoes him. He starts asking whether he's been defending the gospel or only defending the Christian town he grew up in. He doesn't find a quick answer. He simply stops fighting for the old world and begins, tentatively, to ask what it would mean to be the church without it. Talk about where his grief was right and where it turned sour, where he confused Christendom with Christ, and what a first step looks like for someone who realizes he's been defending the scaffolding.

sessions.title: A Letter to the Exiles
sessions.aim: To read Jeremiah's letter to the captives in Babylon as a charter for a church living in a culture it doesn't control: not fighting it, not fleeing it, not surrendering to it, but seeking its good while waiting on God.
sessions.summary:
When Judah was carried into exile, the prophets people wanted to hear said it would be brief. Hananiah promised that within two years God would break Babylon's yoke (Jeremiah 28:3). Jeremiah sent a letter that said the opposite: settle in. "Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce" (Jeremiah 29:5). "Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare" (Jeremiah 29:7).

Two reactions are worth hearing. The zealot says that's collaboration, and he's right that exiles must never simply assimilate; Daniel drew lines he wouldn't cross. The assimilationist says we should just blend in, and he's right that the church is sent for the world's good, not its own comfort. Jeremiah forbids both the revolt and the surrender. The exiles are to be fully present and fully distinct at once, and under the instructions is a promise: God is with them in Babylon, not only back in Jerusalem.

keyScripture.why: "Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare" (Jeremiah 29:7). God tells his people to bless the city that conquered them. That's the charter for a church that no longer runs its culture.

discussion.q: The exiles wanted to hear that Babylon would fall fast. Jeremiah told them to settle in for a long stay. Where do you catch yourself waiting for the culture to turn back instead of living faithfully in the one we have?
discussion.behind: Open on the false hope. Many people are quietly waiting for a return to a Christian culture the way the exiles waited to go home. Naming it matters, because the waiting keeps us from doing what Jeremiah commands.

discussion.q: God tells the exiles to pray for Babylon, the city that burned the temple. How do you react to being told to seek the good of a culture that often feels hostile to your faith?
discussion.behind: Let people feel how much this cuts against instinct. Then move toward the logic: the church is sent for the world's good, not only its own survival.

discussion.q: Jeremiah rules out both fighting Babylon and blending into it. Which of those is the bigger temptation for you, and why?
discussion.behind: Most people lean one way. Help each person find their own pull, because naming it is the first defense against it.

discussion.q: Daniel served the empire well and still refused the king's food and kept praying when it was outlawed. Where are the lines you must not cross, and where are you free, even called, to invest in the common good?
discussion.behind: Move from theory to discernment. Help the room tell the places of free engagement from the places of necessary refusal, without making everything a battle or giving everything away.

discussion.q: Have you treated the present as a delay to wait out instead of the place God has actually sent you? What has that cost?
discussion.behind: Bring it home, starting with yourself. The hardest thing is to stop waiting for the old world and start living in the real one.

objections.objection: Seeking Babylon's welfare is just collaboration. The faithful should resist the godless city, not water its gardens and pray for it. Jeremiah is counseling surrender.
objections.response: The concern is real: exiles must never simply assimilate. Daniel served Babylon and still refused the king's food and faced the lions rather than stop praying. A church that crosses every line has stopped being the church. But read the letter closely. Jeremiah isn't telling the exiles to become Babylonian. He's telling them to live there without revolt, to build and plant and pray for the city while remaining plainly the Lord's people. Seeking the welfare of a city isn't adopting its gods. It's the patient work of people who love their neighbors enough to pray for them, and it's how a watching world gets drawn to a God it doesn't yet know.

objections.objection: If we're supposed to seek the culture's welfare, we should stop being so different and just blend in. Distinctiveness only makes us look hostile and strange.
objections.response: The church really is sent for the world's good, and a sour, withdrawn faith betrays that. But the same letter assumes the exiles stay unmistakably the people of God, and the good they bring Babylon depends on their not becoming Babylonian. A church that looks exactly like its culture has nothing to give it. Jesus called that salt that has lost its taste (Matthew 5:13). The early Christians sought the good of the empire precisely by refusing its idols. Blend in entirely and you don't bless the city. You disappear into it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God has sent you on purpose into the exact place you live, not as a punishment but as an assignment, what would it mean to stop waiting to leave and start seeking its good?
sessions.practice: This week, do one concrete thing for the good of the place God has put you: your street, your workplace, your town. Make it something that isn't aimed at winning an argument or recruiting anyone. Pray for that place by name, including the people in it you find hardest to love. Then notice your own heart. Did it feel like betrayal, like duty, or like the odd freedom of an exile who knows God is here too?
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you told the captives in Babylon to build and plant and seek the good of the city that had carried them off, because you were with them there. You've told us the same. We confess we've been waiting to go home to a world that's gone, and we haven't learned to live well in the one you gave us. Forgive us the revolt that hates our neighbors and the surrender that forgets your name. Teach us to be present and distinct at once, to seek the good of this place without bowing to its gods, and to trust that you have a future and a hope for us here, with you. Amen.
reflection: Have I been treating my culture as a place to escape or fight, instead of a place God has sent me to seek its welfare?
Where am I tempted to revolt, and where am I tempted to blend in? What would it look like to refuse both?
If God was with his people in Babylon and not only in Jerusalem, where is he with me in the very exile I keep wishing were over?
sessions.teaching:
When the people of Judah were marched into Babylon, they were desperate for a word of hope, and there were prophets happy to give them the one they wanted. Hananiah stood in the temple and announced that within two years God would break the king of Babylon's yoke and bring everything home (Jeremiah 28:3). Hold on, don't get comfortable, this is temporary. Then Jeremiah sent a letter to the exiles that said almost the opposite.

"Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters" (Jeremiah 29:5-6). Multiply there, and don't dwindle. And then the line that must have stunned them: "Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare" (Jeremiah 29:7). Notice who does the sending. Nebuchadnezzar thought he had carried them off. God says, I sent you. Why would he tell a conquered people to invest in the city that burned their temple?

The zealot hears collaboration. A faithful people should resist Babylon and never water its gardens. He has a point: exiles must never simply assimilate. The same Babylon gives us Daniel, who served the empire with excellence and still drew lines he'd die before crossing. "Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food" (Daniel 1:8), and when prayer was outlawed he went home and knelt by his open window "as he had done previously" (Daniel 6:10). A people who cross every line have stopped being the people of God.

The assimilationist hears the opposite. If we're told to seek the city's good, then let's stop being so different and blend in. He has a point too. The church really is sent for the good of the world and not just its own survival, and a bitter, withdrawn faith betrays the very thing Jeremiah describes.

Jeremiah won't let either one have the field. He forbids the revolt: the exiles aren't told to fight Babylon or wait sullenly for it to fall. They're told to build, plant, and pray. And he forbids the surrender: the whole letter assumes they stay unmistakably the Lord's. The good they bring to Babylon depends on their not becoming Babylonian. Fully present and fully distinct at the same time is the hardest posture there is, and it's the one the church after Christendom is being handed.

Underneath all the practical instruction is a promise. "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). We've put that verse on greeting cards, but it was written to exiles who had lost everything and had just been told the exile would last seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10), which meant most of them would die in Babylon. Its comfort wasn't that the exile would be cancelled. It was that God had plans inside Babylon, that the place of their loss was also a place of his presence.

Many of us have missed this. We've preached and prayed as if the exile were a short inconvenience, as if the right strategy or the right election would bring the old world back, so we never learned to live where God had actually put us. We kept the church waiting at the window for a Jerusalem that wasn't coming, while God was saying, plant a garden here, because I'm here too.

scriptureStudy.note: "Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce." God tells the exiles to invest in ordinary life in Babylon, not to treat it as a waiting room.
"In its welfare you will find your welfare." The exiles' good is tied to the good of the city that conquered them.
"Do not let your prophets and your diviners who are among you deceive you." The lie was the promise of a quick return, the very thing people most wanted to hear.
"Plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope." Written to people told to settle into a long loss, it promises God's presence in Babylon, not escape from it.
"Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food." He served the empire well and still kept a line, present without being absorbed.
He prayed "as he had done previously." Daniel stayed distinct when distinctiveness was made illegal, without taking up arms.
"When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you." The exile was long, a lifetime for many, and still bounded by God's faithfulness.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, trace exile through the whole Bible, because Jeremiah's letter isn't an isolated piece of advice. Israel is formed in Egypt, a land not its own, and made a distinct people at Sinai. In Babylon and Persia, Daniel, Esther, and Nehemiah work out what it means to serve a foreign power without bowing to it. By the New Testament it's the church's basic self-understanding: Peter writes to "elect exiles," and Hebrews says "here we have no lasting city" (Hebrews 13:14).

An anonymous early Christian writing, the Letter to Diognetus, describes Christians as living in their own countries only as sojourners, sharing in everything as citizens and enduring everything as foreigners (paraphrased). Set that beside the Christendom centuries, when the church largely forgot it was an exilic people and came to think of itself as the establishment. What feels like a frightening new condition is the church's oldest one.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a Christian teacher in a public school finds that what she once took for granted has evaporated: the shared moral vocabulary, the sense that her faith was respectable, the easy overlap between being a good teacher and being a good Christian. Her first instinct is to fight every change. It makes her bitter, and her students feel it. Exhausted, she goes the other way and keeps her faith completely private, and she feels as if she's disappeared.

Then an older believer points her to Jeremiah's letter and asks what it would mean to seek the welfare of her school the way the exiles were told to seek Babylon's. She stops fighting the institution and stops hiding in it. She becomes the teacher who stays late for the struggling kid, who won't join the cruelty in the staff room, who prays by name for colleagues she finds hard to like. She keeps a few clear lines, like Daniel, and otherwise gives herself to the good of the place. Eventually a few students ask what makes her different. Use her to help the group find their own pull toward revolt or surrender, and to picture what seeking the welfare of their own Babylon would take.
