sessions.title: Witness Without Power
sessions.aim: To recover the early church's way of bearing witness: not by seizing or defending cultural power, but by the patient attractiveness of a community whose life can't be explained apart from Christ.
sessions.summary:
For a long time the church in the West could count on the culture to back up its message. That's gone. So how does the church bear witness when it can't legislate its convictions or rely on the culture to make faith plausible?

One answer says seize what power you can: vote, win the courts, take back the institutions. It's right that Christians may not retreat into a private faith. The other says abandon the public square and tend your own garden. It's right that the church's deepest work is forming a holy people, not managing a nation.

The early church refutes both. It had no power and still converted an empire, and it was anything but hidden: it stayed in plague-stricken cities and cared for the sick when others fled. Lesslie Newbigin argued that the congregation itself is the "hermeneutic of the gospel," the lens through which the world reads the good news. Power can compel, but it can't convert.

keyScripture.why: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13:35). Jesus names the church's love, not its power, as the evidence the world reads.

discussion.q: For generations the culture helped the church make its case. Now it doesn't. How have you felt that change?
discussion.behind: Many people feel suddenly exposed, having to explain what used to be assumed. Name the disorientation before turning to what witness looks like without the backup.

discussion.q: What's right in the instinct to vote hard, litigate, and win back institutions? Where does it go wrong as a strategy for witness?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Public engagement is legitimate; Christians may not hide. The error is treating power as the engine of witness when the early church had none.

discussion.q: Newbigin said the congregation is the lens through which the world reads the gospel. If that's true, what does our life together say?
discussion.behind: We tend to think witness is words and arguments. Newbigin moves it to the visible life of the church. Let the room feel the weight of that.

discussion.q: Read Acts 2:44-47. The early church shared what it had, cared for the sick in plagues, and had "favor with all the people." What would that kind of costly, visible love look like where you live?
discussion.behind: Move from idea to imagination. Help the room picture specific, costly presence in their actual town, the kind that makes outsiders ask what could explain it.

discussion.q: Where do you reach for the faster, stronger-looking lever because the slow work of simply living the gospel feels too weak to matter?
discussion.behind: Bring it home, starting with yourself. The patient way feels weak, and we grab for power because it promises faster results.

objections.objection: Witness without power is witness that gets ignored. If we give up the courts, the schools, and the laws, the culture will roll right over us. We have to fight for influence.
objections.response: Christians may not retreat into a private faith, and public engagement is part of loving the world. Withdrawal isn't humility. But the early church had no courts, no schools, no laws, and no votes, and nobody ignored it. It changed an empire from a position of complete powerlessness, by a way of life so different the world couldn't look away. When the church puts its hope in seizing influence, it tends to get the influence and lose the witness, and becomes one more faction grabbing for advantage. The deepest public witness it ever offered was a people whose love for the unloved made no sense unless the gospel were true.

objections.objection: The church should get out of the public square and the culture wars entirely. Engagement only makes us look angry and political.
objections.response: The reaction is understandable and partly right. A faith that becomes mostly a political program has lost its center. But total withdrawal isn't the early church either. That church stayed in the cities during epidemics to nurse the sick, including strangers, when many who could afford to fled. It built a public life of mercy everyone could see. Jesus said a city on a hill can't be hidden (Matthew 5:14). The answer to angry, power-hungry engagement isn't absence. It's a different kind of presence: costly, visible, and impossible to mistake for a bid for power.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the only argument for the gospel your neighbors could see were the life of your church and your own life in it, what would they conclude?
sessions.practice: This week, offer one small witness that has no power in it, something that can't coerce and can only attract. Do a visible kindness for someone outside the faith with nothing attached: no pitch, no agenda. Resist the urge to explain it. Then think about the difference between trying to win someone and simply loving them, and write down what you noticed in yourself.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you said the world would know we're yours by our love for one another, not by our power over the culture, and we've so often reached for the power instead. Forgive us for trusting the courts and the votes and the arguments more than the slow, costly love that drew people to you in the beginning. You won the world from a manger and a cross. Make us a community whose life can't be explained apart from you, present in the suffering around us, distinct in our love, content to attract rather than compel. Let our neighbors read the gospel in us. Amen.
reflection: Where have I assumed the church needs cultural or political power to be heard?
If outsiders read the gospel mainly through the life of my church, what are they reading right now?
Where am I reaching for the fast lever of influence instead of the slow work of living the gospel where I am?
sessions.teaching:
For a long time the church in the West could assume the culture would help it make its case. The laws leaned its way. The schools taught a broadly Christian morality. Religion was respectable, so the church rarely had to do the hard work of persuasion; the culture did much of it, carrying people toward belief on a current of social habit. That's gone, and one of the most disorienting things about the present is that we suddenly have to explain what we used to assume. So how does a church bear witness when it can't legislate its convictions or count on the culture to make faith plausible?

One answer says seize what power you can. Vote hard, win the courts, take back the institutions, because witness without influence gets ignored. There's truth in that. The church may not retreat into a private faith and let the world go. Christians are sent into public life, and abandoning it isn't humility.

The other answer says get out. The culture wars make the church look angry and political, so go quiet, tend your own garden, and let the world go where it will. There's truth here too. The church's deepest work really is forming a holy people, not managing a nation, and a faith that becomes mostly a political program has lost its center.

The early church answers both. It had no power at all: no courts, no schools, no votes, no respectability. It was an illegal, suspected, often persecuted minority, and it converted the empire anyway, from the bottom up. But it wasn't hiding. When epidemics swept the Roman cities and those who could afford it fled, Christians stayed and nursed the sick, including people who weren't Christians, and some of them caught the disease and died. Their witness wasn't a private spirituality. It was a public life of mercy that everyone could see and no one could quite explain. Luke says of the first believers that they shared what they had, ate together "with glad and generous hearts," and had "favor with all the people" (Acts 2:46-47).

Lesslie Newbigin spent most of his working life as a missionary in India, and when he came back to Britain he saw the West as a mission field. His conclusion was that in a culture that no longer believes the gospel, the only real defense of it is a congregation that lives it. He called the congregation the "hermeneutic of the gospel," the lens through which a watching world reads what the good news means. People usually don't believe the message first and then join the community. More often they meet the community, find its life hard to explain, and are drawn through it to the Lord who explains it.

That changes how we should feel about our weakness. Witness without power isn't a lesser version of witness with power. It's the original, and it's stronger, because power can compel but it can't convert. Law and social pressure can produce conformity, crowds of people who go along because going along is easy, which is what Christendom produced. A faith that can't coerce can only attract, and only that kind ever changed anyone from the inside. "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13:35).

I haven't always believed that, not really. The slow work of being a community that simply lives the gospel feels too weak to matter, so I've reached for the faster lever: the vote, the argument, the influence I can grab. It can feel like bringing a candle to a war. But the candle was the point. The question for us isn't how to recover our power. It's whether we're willing to become, again, a community whose life can't be explained apart from Christ.

scriptureStudy.note: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Jesus names love among his people, not power or argument, as the evidence the world reads.
"Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven." Witness is visible and public, but the glory goes to God.
"Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds." Peter assumes a hostile audience and stakes the witness on conduct.
"Always being prepared to make a defense ... for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect." Bold, but never coercive.
"God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong." A powerless church isn't a defeated one; it's where God has always worked.
"My power is made perfect in weakness." The absence of worldly strength is where God's power shows most clearly.

They ate together "with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day." The church grew through the visible life it shared.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at how the early church actually grew. We tend to picture mass preaching and dramatic events. Alan Kreider, in The Patient Ferment of the Early Church, tells a slower story: for long stretches there were no church buildings, no advertising, no political access, and a demanding formation before baptism that could last years. Yet the church grew steadily, and Kreider argues it grew because it was patient, forming people into a way of life so distinct that outsiders noticed.

The sociologist Rodney Stark, in The Rise of Christianity (1996), points to the church's conduct during the great epidemics of the second and third centuries, when Christians cared for the sick, their own and others, and argues that both their survival rates and their reputation rose as a result. Set that beside how many churches now think about growth: fast, programmatic, measured in crowds and influence. Ask whether we still believe the slow way works, and whether losing our power might return us to the methods that worked before we had any.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a small congregation in a neighborhood that has written off the church decides to stop arguing with its neighbors and simply serve them, with no strings attached. There's no big event or campaign. They go quietly to the places where people are hurting. They sit with a widower nobody visits. They take meals to an exhausted single mother who has never set foot in their building and won't be pressured to. They help clean up after a flood for people who are openly hostile to their faith. When a neighbor finally asks, half suspicious, what they want out of it, the answer is nothing; they're trying to love the way Jesus loved them.

It costs them, and for a long time attendance doesn't move. The pastor nearly gives up a dozen times because it feels too weak to matter. But over years the neighborhood's hostility softens into curiosity, and a few people who can't account for love that asks nothing back start asking about the One behind it. Use this to talk about the difference between trying to win people and simply loving them, and where that kind of patient love might be possible in your own setting.

memoryVerse.text: By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.

sessions.title: A Creative Minority
sessions.aim: To stop thinking of the church as a defeated majority and recover its calling as a creative minority: a small, distinct people whose joyful difference becomes a gift to a world that no longer shares its faith.
sessions.summary:
When a people used to being the majority become a minority, they usually choose one of two postures. They become defensive, bitter and besieged and defined by what they've lost. Or they assimilate, dissolving into the culture until nothing distinct is left. There's a third way, and it has a name: a creative minority, a small people who accept that they're small, refuse both bitterness and dissolution, and turn their difference into a gift for the common good.

Two objections deserve a hearing. One says a minority can't shape a culture, and it's right that the church is losing size and status. The other says distinctiveness is just a holy huddle, and it's right that distinctiveness can turn self-righteous. But smallness isn't irrelevance, and distinctiveness isn't withdrawal. The early church's strange disciplines, its refusal to abandon infants, its care for the poor, the stranger and the dying, were a gift to its world. The church isn't being asked to win. It's being asked to be good, and so distinct that its goodness becomes a gift.

keyScripture.why: "You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored?" (Matthew 5:13). Salt is useful because it's unlike what it's mixed into. A small amount changes the whole.

discussion.q: A shrinking majority usually turns bitter and defensive, or quietly dissolves. Which do you see more in the church around you, and which pulls harder on you?
discussion.behind: Name both failures first, so the idea of a creative minority lands as a real alternative and not a slogan.

discussion.q: What's the difference between being distinct for the world and being distinct against it?
discussion.behind: The same practice can bless or wall out, depending on the heart behind it. Help the room feel the difference between a huddle that hoards and a difference that gives.

discussion.q: The early church refused to abandon unwanted infants, cared for the poor and the dying, and kept a different ethic of money and sex. That made it odd. What disciplines might make the church oddly good now?
discussion.behind: Push for specific, present-day examples that would make the church both distinct and good, not just different for its own sake.

discussion.q: Read Deuteronomy 7:7. God says he chose Israel when they were "the fewest of all peoples." What does that say to the fear that a smaller church is a defeated church?
discussion.behind: We equate influence with size. Scripture and history both argue otherwise. Help the room separate faithfulness from numbers.

discussion.q: Where do you measure faithfulness, in your church or your own life, by size? What would change if you measured it by depth?
discussion.behind: Bring it home, starting with yourself. The hunger for size often dresses up as a hunger for impact. The point is reordering toward depth, not despising growth.

objections.objection: A minority can't shape a culture. Influence takes numbers, and a shrinking church is simply a losing one, whatever you call it.
objections.response: The church in the West is losing size and status, and pretending otherwise is denial. But the idea that influence requires numbers doesn't survive history. The Jewish people have shaped the law, ethics, and moral imagination of whole civilizations while remaining a small fraction of the population, by being distinct rather than by being many. The early church was a tiny share of the Roman Empire and reshaped it from below. A creative minority doesn't outvote a culture; it out-lives it. A small, distinct, good church can shape a culture in ways a large, bland one never could.

objections.objection: All this talk of distinctiveness is a polite name for sectarian withdrawal, a holy huddle that abandons the world.
objections.response: The danger is real. Distinctiveness can turn into a smug, withdrawn separatism that hoards its holiness and looks down on everyone outside, and the church has done exactly that. But that's the corruption of distinctiveness, not its nature. A creative minority is distinct for the sake of the world. The early church's refusals, of abandoning infants, of treating the poor and the sick as disposable, weren't a wall to keep the world out. They were a gift to a world that hadn't seen such things, and much of what the West later took for granted about the dignity of the weak grew from them. The test is whether our difference makes us a gift or a fortress.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your church became much smaller but more distinct, more costly to belong to and more clearly good, would you feel that as a defeat or as a kind of freedom?
sessions.practice: This week, practice one discipline that makes you different in a way that serves rather than separates: generosity that doesn't make sense, forgiveness the world would call foolish, refusing a cruelty everyone else accepts, or time with someone others have written off. Do it as a gift, not to make a point. Then ask whether your difference felt like a wall you put up or a gift you gave.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we've been afraid of becoming small, as if the worth of your church were measured in crowds, and we've hidden that fear behind talk of impact. Forgive us for wanting to be many more than we wanted to be holy. Teach us to be a creative minority: distinct without bitterness, present without dissolving, good in a way that blesses a world that no longer shares our faith. Make us salt that hasn't lost its taste and light that isn't hidden, the way your early church blessed an empire it could never have outvoted. Amen.
reflection: Am I more tempted toward the bitter, defensive minority or the quietly assimilated one, and what would the third way ask me to lay down?
Where is my distinctiveness a gift to others, and where has it become a fortress?
Where have I measured faithfulness by size, and what would change if I measured it by depth and by the quality of our love?
sessions.teaching:
When people who are used to being the majority become a minority, they almost always reach for one of two postures, and both are slow ways to die. The first is the defensive minority. It turns bitter and besieged, defined more by what it has lost than by what it believes, resentful toward whoever it blames for the loss, fighting a long rearguard action with the doors shut. It survives for a while, but it survives as a grievance, and a grievance has never converted anyone.

The second is the assimilated minority. It quietly stops being different. It keeps the vocabulary and loses the substance, until there's nothing distinct left and it disappears into the world it was supposed to bless.

There's a third way, and it has a name worth keeping: a creative minority. That's a small people who accept that they're small, who refuse both bitterness and dissolution, and who turn their very difference into a gift. They don't resent the world and they don't melt into it. They bless it by staying themselves.

Two objections deserve a fair hearing. The first says a minority can't shape a culture; influence takes numbers, and a shrinking church is a losing church. There's a hard fact under that, because the church in the West really is losing size and status. But the premise is false. The Jewish people have shaped the law, ethics, and moral imagination of whole civilizations while remaining a small fraction of the population, by holding a covenant, a memory, and a way of life that wouldn't dissolve. God told Israel he chose them not "because you were more in number than any other people ... for you were the fewest of all peoples" (Deuteronomy 7:7). The early church was a tiny share of the Roman Empire, and it reshaped that empire from below.

The second objection says distinctiveness is a polite name for withdrawal, a holy huddle that abandons the world. That danger is real too. Distinctiveness can turn into a smug separatism that hoards its holiness, and the church has done it. But that's the corruption of distinctiveness, not its nature. A creative minority is distinct for the sake of the world, and that makes all the difference.

Look at the early church again, a creative minority before anyone used the phrase. In a world where unwanted infants were often abandoned to die, Christians refused to do it, and some took in children others had left. In a world that treated the poor, the sick, and the dying as disposable, they built a network of care for exactly those people, including strangers. In a world of casual cruelty, they kept a discipline about the body, marriage, and the weak that their neighbors found bizarre. Those weren't walls to keep the world out. They were a gift to a world that hadn't seen such things, and much of what the West later called humane, the dignity of the weak, the infant, and the stranger that even secular people now assume, grew from that soil. A minority's difference became a majority's inheritance, not by force but by a way of life that turned out to be more humane than anything the culture had on its own.

We have to own our part here, because the church has measured nearly everything by size. A smaller, more distinct, more costly church feels like failure to us. Many of us absorbed the idea that bigger means better without noticing, and we called the hunger for size a hunger for impact. The end of Christendom is curing us of that, slowly and against our will. The church after Christendom isn't being asked to win. It's being asked to be good, and small, and so distinct that its goodness becomes a gift the world can't account for. That isn't defeat. It's the church's oldest vocation, handed back to us just when we're small enough to receive it.

scriptureStudy.note: "You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored?" Salt works by being unlike what it's mixed into. Lose that and it's good for nothing.
The mustard seed is "the smallest of all seeds," and leaven is hidden in flour. Jesus describes a kingdom that works from small and hidden places, not from dominance.
"But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession." The church is a distinct people, which is where any creative minority starts.
"For you were the fewest of all peoples." Israel's calling never depended on its size.
"Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind." Refusing conformity is what keeps a minority from dissolving.
"There was not a needy person among them." The early church's shared economic life made it strange and good at the same time.
"Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land." Jeremiah buys a field with an army at the gates, a small act of hope planted in the middle of loss.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, trace where the phrase "creative minority" comes from. The historian Arnold Toynbee used it for the small groups that, in his account, renew a civilization by answering a crisis with a new way of life that others later imitate. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, who was Chief Rabbi of Britain, applied it to the Jewish people and to religious communities in the modern West, notably in a 2013 lecture, "On Creative Minorities": distinct enough to keep a way of life, generous enough to bless the wider world, and resisting both the defensive enclave and assimilation.

Set that beside Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon's Resident Aliens (1989), which argues that the church's first political task is simply to be the church, and beside the monasteries that kept learning, farming, and prayer alive in small disciplined communities after Rome fell. Weigh both the promise and the danger. The promise is that the church needn't be large or powerful to matter. The danger is that "creative minority" becomes a comforting label for a church that is merely shrinking, or a cover for a huddle that has stopped loving its neighbors.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose two churches in the same city face the same decline and take opposite roads. The first decides survival means becoming as much like the surrounding culture as possible. It smooths away anything strange or demanding until belonging asks almost nothing. Within a decade it has nothing distinct to offer, and it quietly empties out.

The second, smaller and more frightened at first, goes deeper instead of thinner. It asks more of its people: a shared rhythm of prayer, serious generosity, a refusal of certain cruelties the city takes for granted, and a commitment to the people the city has discarded, the addicted, the elderly with no family, the kids the system has given up on. For a while it gets even smaller. But neighbors who share none of its beliefs start to respect it, then rely on it, and some begin to wonder where it comes from. It never grows large, but it becomes a presence far beyond its size. Talk about why the first church died trying to survive and the second found life by becoming more distinct, and which road your own church and your own discipleship are on.

memoryVerse.text: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet.

sessions.title: Hope Without Nostalgia
sessions.aim: To ground the church's hope in the God who is bringing a future rather than in recovering a Christian past, and to send the exiles out to live well now, neither mourning what's gone nor despairing of what's coming.
sessions.summary:
When a familiar world ends, the heart reaches backward. The church after Christendom is tempted by nostalgia, the ache to return to a remembered golden age when everything was Christian and ordered and ours. Is that ache hope, or hope's counterfeit?

The nostalgic says the past really was better and the way forward is back, and he's right that real goods have been lost. The progressive says the past was never that good, so embrace whatever comes next, and she's right that the golden age is partly a trick of memory. But nostalgia isn't hope; Christian hope has never pointed back to a lost golden age. And mere acceptance of the future isn't hope either. Hope is confident expectation of a particular future that God himself is bringing.

The exiles weren't promised the old Jerusalem back unchanged. They were given "a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). The church doesn't need its old world back. It needs its Lord, who never depended on a Christian culture to do his work.

keyScripture.why: "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). Spoken to exiles told to settle into their loss, it grounds hope in the God who is bringing a future, not in a restored past.

discussion.q: Where do you feel the pull of nostalgia for a more Christian time? What exactly are you aching to get back?
discussion.behind: Get the specific longing on the table, the Sunday closings, the cultural backing, the ease, so the room can ask later whether that ache is hope or its counterfeit.

discussion.q: What's the difference between longing to go back to a Christian past and hoping forward to a kingdom God is bringing?
discussion.behind: Nostalgia looks back; hope looks forward. Confusing them keeps a church mourning instead of living and working.

discussion.q: The past was never as good as we remember, and real goods were still lost. How do you hold both?
discussion.behind: The room will tend either to gild the past or dismiss it. Help people grieve real losses without making the past an idol.

discussion.q: Read Isaiah 43:18-19. God says, "Behold, I am doing a new thing." What would it mean for you to hope for something God is bringing that you can't yet picture?
discussion.behind: We want the specific old thing back, and God offers a future we can't see yet. Let the room sit with both the discomfort and the freedom of that.

discussion.q: Looking back over all five sessions, what's the one thing from the old world you most need to stop carrying, and what would setting it down free you to do?
discussion.behind: Close the study by bringing it home, starting with yourself. Don't resolve it; end facing forward.

objections.objection: The past really was better. Families were intact, the culture made faith easy, and children knew right from wrong. The way forward is back; anything else is surrender to decline.
objections.response: More of this is true than a cynic expects. Real goods have been lost, not every change is progress, and a culture that has forgotten the gospel is harsher in measurable ways. But two things need saying. First, the golden age is partly a trick of memory. That same culture lived alongside injustices it baptized and nominal faith it produced, and we tend to remember the order and forget the rot. Second, and more important, even where the past was better, Christian hope has never pointed backward. It points to a kingdom coming. Making the recovery of the past the object of the church's hope aims hope in the wrong direction. Grieve the losses. Don't make the past the thing you hope for.

objections.objection: The past was never as good as people remember, so stop mourning it and embrace the future. Progress is real, and clinging to the old world is the whole problem.
objections.response: The golden age is largely a trick of memory, and clinging to a romanticized past is a real idolatry. But mere acceptance of the future isn't hope. The assumption that whatever comes next is better because it's next isn't supported by history, which is full of changes that made the world worse. Hope isn't general optimism. It's confident expectation of a particular future that God is bringing: his kingdom, his new creation. The person who simply embraces the future has no more ground for confidence than the one who clings to the past. Both have cut hope loose from the God who holds both.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your hope for the church rested entirely on what God is bringing and not on getting any part of the old world back, what would you stop grieving, and what would you be free to start building?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing that belongs to the future God is bringing rather than the past you're mourning. Plant something, literally or otherwise, that you may not see bear fruit: an investment in a person, a piece of work, a place. Each time you catch yourself aching for the old world, turn the ache into a prayer for the kingdom that's coming, and write down what changes in you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you didn't promise the exiles the old world back. You promised them yourself, present in Babylon, and a future they couldn't yet see. We confess we've spent our grief facing backward, mourning a Christendom that's gone, while you've been calling us forward. Heal us of the nostalgia that passes for faith. Teach us a hope that doesn't depend on getting anything back, that rests on you, who were making all things new long before any of this began and will be long after it's forgotten. Send us out to build and plant and bless and love, because you are ahead of us, bringing your kingdom. Amen.
reflection: Have I confused nostalgia for a Christian past with Christian hope?
What am I still clutching from the old world that I need to set down to live well in this one?
If my hope rested entirely on the God who is making all things new, what would I stop mourning, and what would I be free to begin?
sessions.teaching:
We've spent four sessions on the end of Christendom and on the church's old calling as an exilic, creative minority that bears witness without power. There's one last thing to face, because it can quietly undo all the rest: nostalgia. When a familiar world ends, the heart reaches backward. The church after Christendom is tempted by a strong and corrosive longing for a remembered golden age, when everything was Christian and ordered and ours, when stores closed on Sunday and believing cost nothing. Is that ache hope, or is it hope's most convincing counterfeit?

The nostalgic says the past really was better. Families were more intact, the culture made faith easier, children grew up with a shared sense of right and wrong, and the way forward is back. More of that is true than you might expect. Real goods have been lost. Not every change is progress, and a culture that has forgotten the gospel is harsher in measurable ways than one that remembered it. A study that pretended otherwise would be lying to make you comfortable.

The progressive says the past was never that good, so stop mourning and embrace whatever comes next. There's truth there too. The golden age is largely a trick of memory. That Christian culture lived alongside injustices it blessed and nominal faith it manufactured, and we're very good at remembering its order and forgetting its rot.

Here's where it turns. Nostalgia isn't hope, because Christian hope has never pointed backward to a lost golden age, not even to Eden. The Bible doesn't end with a return to the garden. It ends with a city coming down out of heaven and a voice saying, "Behold, I am making all things new" (Revelation 21:5). God told his people through Isaiah, "Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old. Behold, I am doing a new thing" (Isaiah 43:18-19). Making the recovery of Christendom the object of our hope spends the energy of the future grieving the past. But simply accepting the future isn't hope either. The confidence that whatever is next is better because it's next isn't Christian, and history doesn't support it. Hope is confident expectation of a particular future that God himself is bringing.

That's what the exiles were given. Remember who Jeremiah 29:11 was written to. Not people on their way up, but people who had lost everything and had just been told to build houses in Babylon and stay a lifetime. The hope they received wasn't the old Jerusalem restored unchanged. It was a future they couldn't yet see, resting entirely on the God who was with them in exile.

So the study doesn't land on a strategy. Christian hope runs forward. It rests on a kingdom coming, on a God who was making all things new long before Constantine made the faith respectable and will be long after the last great cathedral in the West has become a museum. The church doesn't need its old world back. It never did. It needs its Lord, who built his church under Nero with no power, no respectability and no Sunday laws, and who is doing the same thing again in the ruins of the arrangement we're mourning.

Many of us have grieved this loss facing the wrong way. We've prayed more for the old world to come back than for the kingdom to come, and we've called that faithfulness. We've stood at the window like the exiles, waiting for a Jerusalem that wasn't coming, while the word the whole time was: turn around, I'm ahead of you, build here. So I'll end the way Jeremiah ended his letter, by sending you out to live. Build your houses. Plant your gardens. Seek the welfare of the city. Bear your witness by a love no one can explain. Paul put it simply: "forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on" (Philippians 3:13-14). The God who is ahead of us isn't finished.

scriptureStudy.note: "To give you a future and a hope." Spoken to exiles told to settle into a long loss, it grounds hope in the God who holds the future, not in a restored past.
"Remember not the former things ... Behold, I am doing a new thing." God tells his people to stop facing backward, because his work is ahead of them.
"Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal." Paul refuses to live in even a glorious past.
They "acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth" and desired "a better country, that is, a heavenly one." The faithful didn't long to go back; they looked ahead.
"Behold, I am making all things new." The Bible ends with new creation, not a return to a lost garden.
"No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." A sharp word against the backward look that freezes us.
"Now hope that is seen is not hope." Hope is for what isn't yet visible, so it can't be the recovery of a remembered past.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, name the kind of age we live in. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in A Secular Age (2007), argues that the deepest change in the modern West isn't simply that fewer people believe, but that the conditions of belief have shifted. Faith has gone from the unquestioned default to one contested option among many, and every position feels fragile under what he calls cross-pressures. That's why the church's loss feels like a loss of plausibility, not only of numbers.

Then read Augustine beside him. After the Goths sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed the Christians, and Augustine answered with The City of God. He refused both the pagan nostalgia and the Christian triumphalism that confused the empire with the kingdom, and he taught the church to see two cities intermingled through history, setting its hope on the city of God and not on any earthly order, however Christian it looked. Taylor names our condition; Augustine, at the end of an earlier Christian-seeming world, names the hope that survives it.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose an older believer, faithful his whole life, slides into a quiet despair as he watches the church and culture he knew come apart. He keeps telling his grandson that everything was better before and there's nothing left to do but hold on and mourn. The grandson, who loves Jesus but never knew the world the old man misses, finally says, "Grandpa, you talk about the church like it already died. The church I'm part of is alive. It's just different, and that scares you."

Over the next weeks the old man notices that his grief always faces backward, that he prays more for the past to return than for the kingdom to come. He doesn't get the old world back, and he stops asking for it. When his hope turns forward, the despair begins to lift, not because the losses weren't real but because they're no longer the last word. He spends his last years investing in the young people of that strange new church, planting things he won't see grow. Use him to help the group tell nostalgia from hope, and to name what each of them is being invited to plant.

memoryVerse.text: For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.

leaderPrimer:
Someone in your group wants their country back. They may say it in those words, or just carry it: the ache for stores closed on Sunday, prayer before kickoff, a world where the culture did half the church's work. Nostalgia is the hazard in this room, and it's subtle because it looks like faithfulness.

You'll be tempted to handle it one of two cheap ways. You can join the funeral and spend five weeks mourning together, which feels pastoral and forms nobody. Or you can sneer, playing the enlightened guide correcting sentimental people, which loses the room in an evening. Don't do either. The grief is real, some of what died deserves mourning, and the study's whole argument is that Christendom was an arrangement and not the faith. Hold the loss and the hope in the same hand.

Watch for two people. The angry one, for whom every session sounds like surrender, needs to hear that exile isn't defeat; Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses and plant gardens in Babylon precisely because God wasn't finished with them (Jeremiah 29). The relieved one, often younger and glad to see cultural Christianity go, needs the harder word that contempt isn't a posture either. Nobody builds a creative minority out of scorn for their grandparents.

Sessions four and five carry the constructive weight, so don't let the group spend itself on lament before it gets there. The aim is a room that stops asking how to get the old world back and starts asking what faithfulness looks like in the one that exists.

faq.q: Is this study telling Christians to give up and accept cultural defeat?
faq.a: No. What's ending is a cultural arrangement, the centuries-long situation in which the surrounding society did much of the church's work and made belief easy and respectable. Real goods are passing with it. But the church isn't ending. The early church had no cultural power and turned the Roman world upside down. The call is to recover that older condition, an exilic, creative minority that bears witness by how it lives, not by the levers of power.

faq.q: Are you saying Christendom was a bad thing?
faq.a: Partly, and partly not. Christendom built hospitals and universities and slowly bent a brutal world toward the memory of a crucified God. It also married the faith to political power, which produced inquisitions and state churches that persecuted dissenters, and it filled pews with people baptized into a culture who were never converted. The study refuses both the nostalgia that remembers only the order and the contempt that remembers only the rot. Grief and relief at once is the right posture.

faq.q: If the culture is hostile, shouldn't we fight to take it back?
faq.a: Christians may not retreat into a private faith, and working for the common good is commanded. But power isn't the engine of witness. The early church had no courts, schools, laws, or votes, and it converted an empire from the bottom up. When the church pours its hope into seizing power, it tends to get the power and lose the witness. The study calls for a costly, visible love that can't coerce and so can only attract.

faq.q: What does it mean to live as exiles? Isn't that a depressing way to see the church?
faq.a: Not once you see where the image comes from. Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon not to revolt and not to assimilate, but to build houses, plant gardens, and seek the welfare of the city, because God was with them there. Exile in that sense isn't exile from God. It's being faithfully present in a culture you don't control. Peter called the church "exiles" in his first sentence. Christendom made the church forget that; its ending gives it back.

faq.q: What's a creative minority, and how is it different from a holy huddle?
faq.a: A creative minority is a small people who accept that they're small, refuse both bitterness and dissolution, and turn their difference into a gift for the wider world. A holy huddle is distinct against the world, hoarding its purity. A creative minority is distinct for the world. The early church's refusal to abandon infants and its care for the poor and the dying weren't a fortress; they were a gift, and much of what the West later called humane grew from them.

faq.q: Is the church doomed because it's shrinking?
faq.a: No. The assumption under the question, that influence requires numbers, doesn't hold up. The Jewish people have shaped whole civilizations while remaining a small fraction of the population. The early church was a tiny share of the Roman Empire and reshaped it. A smaller church isn't automatically a defeated one. It may be freer, released from the temptations of power and respectability and returned to patience, costly love, and the slow formation of a distinct people.

faq.q: Isn't longing for a more Christian past a good thing?
faq.a: The longing is understandable, and real goods have been lost. But nostalgia isn't hope. Christian hope has never pointed back to a lost golden age; the Bible ends with new creation, not a return to Eden. Making the recovery of Christendom the object of our hope spends the future's energy grieving the past. The study asks for grief that faces forward.

faq.q: How is Christian hope different from optimism?
faq.a: Optimism assumes the future will be fine because it's the future, and history doesn't support that. Christian hope is confident expectation of a particular future that God is bringing: his kingdom and new creation. The exiles were given "a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11), grounded in God's faithfulness, not in a general sense that things would improve.

faq.q: Who are the thinkers behind this study, and do I need to know them to lead it?
faq.a: You don't need them to lead it. Charles Taylor describes our time as a secular age in which belief is one contested option among many. Lesslie Newbigin argued that the congregation that lives the gospel is its best defense. Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon argued that the church's first task is to be the church. Alan Kreider described how the early church grew patiently without power. Augustine, writing The City of God after Rome was sacked, taught the church to hope in the city of God and not in any earthly order. The sessions carry everything you need.

faq.q: Does the study expect the church to win the culture back by the end?
faq.a: No, because winning the culture back is the wrong goal. The study ends without a tidy resolution on purpose, since exile doesn't resolve on a schedule. The point is the faithful presence of the church in Christendom's absence: living well in exile, bearing witness without power, hoping forward. The promise isn't a strategy that succeeds but a Lord who is faithful and has never depended on a Christian culture to do his work.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic, and the church losing its grip looks like progress to me. Why should I engage this?
faq.a: It's a fair position, and the study agrees with more of it than you might expect. It grants that Christendom was deeply compromised and that crowds of merely cultural Christians were a problem, not a glory. It doesn't ask you to mourn the church's lost power. What it offers is a claim worth weighing: the church was most humane when it had no power, when it nursed the sick in plague-stricken cities and loved people everyone else despised. You can decide whether a powerless, serving church is worth having around.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm afraid for the future of the church?
faq.a: Your fear doesn't disqualify you, and you don't have to hide it. The study is built to be led by a fellow exile, not by someone who has conquered all anxiety. Every question comes with a note and every session ends in prayer, so you aren't improvising. Admitting your own fear may be the most pastoral thing in the room. What you do need is to keep the study from becoming either a rally or a wake, and to keep pointing everyone, yourself first, toward the God who is ahead of us.

timeline.event: After the first deportation of Judah's leaders to Babylon, Jeremiah writes to the exiles telling them not to revolt and not to assimilate, but to build houses, plant gardens, and seek the welfare of the city (Jeremiah 29). Jerusalem itself falls about ten years later, in 587 or 586 BC.
Daniel serves the Babylonian and then Persian courts while refusing to bow to their gods or stop praying, a picture of an exile who is fully present and fully distinct.
Jesus tells Pilate his kingdom is not of this world, and teaches that his people are salt and light and a city on a hill.
Peter writes to Christians scattered across Asia Minor and addresses them as "elect exiles" and "sojourners," framing the church as a dispersed minority.

Two great epidemics sweep the Roman world. Christian writers of the time describe believers caring for the sick when others fled, and historians have argued this raised the church's reputation and survival.
The Edict of Milan, under Constantine and Licinius, makes Christianity legal across the empire, beginning the long shift in which the church gains power and respectability.
The Goths sack Rome in 410. Augustine answers those who blame the Christians with The City of God, finished about 426, teaching the church to hope in the city of God rather than any earthly order.
Benedict founds the monastery at Monte Cassino. Small disciplined communities living by his Rule preserve learning, prayer, and farming through the collapse of the old order.

Lesslie Newbigin returns to Britain after nearly forty years in India and comes to see the West itself as a mission field. In The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989) he calls the congregation the "hermeneutic of the gospel."
Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon publish Resident Aliens, arguing that the church's first political task is simply to be the church.
Charles Taylor publishes A Secular Age, arguing that the deepest modern change is in the conditions of belief, so that faith has become contested rather than assumed.
Rabbi Jonathan Sacks gives his lecture "On Creative Minorities," applying the idea to religious communities in the modern West.
Alan Kreider publishes The Patient Ferment of the Early Church, describing how the powerless early church grew through patience and a distinct way of life.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. The world we're going to talk about, the one that's ending, is one many of us have feelings about that are hard to say out loud. So, three things before we start. First, you can grieve the passing of a Christian culture here without being called faithless, and you can feel relief at it without being called disloyal. Both are welcome, because both are partly right. Second, this study won't turn into a rally to take the culture back, and it won't turn into a wake for a church that's finished. It's looking for a third way: the patient, hopeful life of people who build and plant and bless the place God has sent them. Third, none of us is outside this. I've leaned on a Christian culture more than on Christ too. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. I'll read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, into the workplace and the neighborhood and the family table where the culture has changed under our feet, because that's where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop here, even though it isn't resolved, because exile doesn't resolve on a schedule. This week, try to carry this toward the kingdom that's coming rather than back toward the world that's gone. Try the practice, and spend some time with the reflection questions on your own. If something tonight has you facing backward, grieving the past more than hoping for the kingdom, take that as a gentle invitation to turn around. God is ahead of us. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, agree that grief and relief are both welcome and that the study will be neither a rally nor a wake, and take session 1's opening questions slowly. Name the difference between Christianity and Christendom.
Week 2: Session 1, The End of Christendom, with extra time on what was good and what was compromised.
Week 3: Session 2, A Letter to the Exiles, part one: Jeremiah's letter and the refusal of both revolt and surrender.
Week 4: Session 2 continued: Daniel as a model of being present and distinct, and the practice of seeking the welfare of a real place.
Week 5: Session 3, Witness Without Power: the early church's costly love and the congregation as the lens for the gospel.
Week 6: Session 4, A Creative Minority: the third way between the defensive and the assimilated minority.
Week 7: Session 5, Hope Without Nostalgia: the difference between nostalgia and hope.
Week 8: Look back over all five practices and the Scripture index, and give each person room to name what they're setting down and what they want to build.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the end of Christendom and the letter to the exiles.
Week 2: Session 3, Witness Without Power, with extra time on the early church's costly love and the difference between attracting and compelling.
Week 4: Session 5, Hope Without Nostalgia, with a short closing conversation facing forward.

bibliography.note: Includes the chapter "The Congregation as Hermeneutic of the Gospel" (1989). The backbone of session 3.

bibliography.title: Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon
bibliography.note: The case that the church is a colony of resident aliens whose first task is to be the church (1989). Sessions 2 and 4.

bibliography.title: The Patient Ferment of the Early Church
bibliography.author: Alan Kreider
bibliography.note: How the early church grew through patience and the slow formation of a distinct way of life (2016). Sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Written after the sack of Rome, refusing both pagan nostalgia and Christian triumphalism. Sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Rise of Christianity
bibliography.author: Rodney Stark
bibliography.note: A sociologist's account of the early church's growth, including its care for the sick during the epidemics (1996). Sessions 3 and 4.

bibliography.title: The Letter to Diognetus
bibliography.author: Anonymous, early Christian
bibliography.note: An early text describing Christians as living in their own countries as sojourners. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: On Creative Minorities
bibliography.author: Jonathan Sacks
bibliography.note: A 2013 lecture applying the idea of the creative minority to religious communities in the modern West. Session 4.

bibliography.title: After Virtue
bibliography.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
bibliography.note: A diagnosis of a fragmented moral culture that ends by calling for new forms of community to sustain virtue (1981). A balancing voice for session 4.

bibliography.title: The Benedict Option
bibliography.author: Rod Dreher
bibliography.note: A widely discussed proposal for distinct Christian community (2017). Useful as a conversation partner to test against the call to bless and not only to withdraw.

bibliography.title: To Change the World
bibliography.author: James Davison Hunter
bibliography.note: On the limits of strategies for cultural power and the alternative Hunter calls "faithful presence" (2010). Session 3.

furtherReading: The Patient Ferment of the Early Church, Alan Kreider, for readers who want to sit longer with how a powerless church grew.
The Gospel in a Pluralist Society, Lesslie Newbigin, for the fuller argument behind session 3.
Resident Aliens, Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon, for anyone wrestling with what it means for the church to be a colony rather than the establishment.
A Secular Age, Charles Taylor, for readers who want to understand why belief itself feels different now.
The City of God, Augustine, to watch the church at the end of an earlier Christian-seeming world learn the hope that survives it.

glossary.definition: The long arrangement, from roughly the fourth century until our own time, in which Christianity was the established religion of a society and the culture did much of the church's work, making belief easy, respectable, and often merely nominal.
Faith carried more by the surrounding society than by personal conversion; being Christian because everyone around you is.

The biblical condition, lived by Judah in Babylon and named by Peter for the church, of living faithfully as a distinct people in a culture you don't control, seeking its welfare while belonging to God.
Peter's picture of the church as "sojourners and exiles," present in a society as good neighbors without finally belonging to it.
A small people who accept that they're small, refuse both bitterness and dissolution, and turn their difference into a gift for the common good.
Bearing witness by a costly, visible way of life that can't coerce and so can only attract, as the early church did.
The change that began when Constantine made Christianity legal and then favored, after which the church gained power and respectability and gradually lost some of what had made it compelling.
The ache to return to a remembered golden age; in this study, hope's counterfeit, because Christian hope points forward.
Not general optimism but confident expectation of a particular future God is bringing, his kingdom and new creation.
Charles Taylor's name for the modern West, where belief has gone from the unquestioned background of life to one contested option among many.
Newbigin's phrase for the local congregation as the lens through which a watching world reads what the gospel means.
Augustine's picture of the city of man and the city of God intermingled through history, teaching the church to hope in the city of God rather than any earthly order.
James Davison Hunter's phrase for being fully and distinctly present in a culture for its good, neither withdrawing from it nor seizing power over it.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: The Christian culture many of us grew up with is ending, and the church keeps reaching for one of two responses: panic that fights to take it all back, or despair that gives up. There's a third way. This five-session study looks at what has actually ended and why it may be a mercy, how Jeremiah taught the exiles in Babylon to live, how the early church bore witness without power, what it means to be a creative minority, and a hope that doesn't run on nostalgia. Any volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Come as you are.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on following Jesus in a world that no longer pretends to be Christian. Before anyone braces: it isn't a rally to win the culture back, and it isn't a wake for a church that's finished. It takes the loss seriously, names what was good and what was compromised, and points us to the church's oldest calling, a small, distinct people who turned the ancient world upside down with no power at all. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. If the changing world has unsettled you, this is for you. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: The early church had no power, no respectability, and no Christian culture behind it, and it turned the world upside down. A five-session study on following Jesus in a post-Christian world. It's clear about what's ending, hopeful about what's coming, and it refuses both panic and despair. Come as you are.
quoteCards: What's ending is not the church. It's the scaffolding. Christendom was never the gospel.
Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses and plant gardens in Babylon, because God was with them there too.
Power can compel, but it can't convert.
Smallness isn't the same as irrelevance. A small, distinct, good church can shape a culture a large, bland one never could.
The early church's difference wasn't a wall it built. It was a gift it gave.
Nostalgia isn't hope. Christian hope has never pointed backward to a lost golden age.
The Bible doesn't end with a return to the garden. It ends with all things made new.
The church doesn't need its old world back. It needs its Lord.
